Active & semiconductor devices › Op-amps

Summing

(formerly Summing amplifier)

What it computes

For the inverting summing amplifier, with two to four inputs (+ add and × on each input's line), it gives: - the output voltage; - each input's weight, shown on its line; - the current through Rf; - where the output clips, from the supply and the op-amp's headroom; - the bandwidth, from the op-amp's gain-bandwidth product.

Source

No standard applies. The output comes from the ideal op-amp model. The headroom and gain-bandwidth figures come from the TL072, LM358 and MCP6002 datasheets, as listed in the Inverting section.

What it means

  • Virtual ground — the op-amp holds its − input at 0 V. So each input drives a current V / R through its own resistor, and is not affected by the others.
  • Adding — those currents meet at the − input, add up, and all flow on through Rf. Rf turns the total into the output voltage, upside down (inverted).
  • Weight — each input's weight is −Rf divided by its own resistor:
  • equal resistors give a plain sum;
  • unequal ones mix channels at different levels, as in an audio mixer;
  • Rf equal to half the input resistors gives the average;
  • binary-weighted resistors (R, 2R, 4R…) make a simple digital-to-analog converter.
  • Headroom — how close the output can get to the supply. It is about 1.5–2 V for a TL072 or LM358, and 0 for a rail-to-rail op-amp. Past that, the output clips.
  • Bandwidth — the op-amp's gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is shared out by the noise gain, 1 + Rf/R1 + Rf/R2 + …. Every input resistor counts, so the bandwidth is lower than any one channel's gain would suggest.

The headroom and GBW entered here are remembered for all the op-amp tools.

Why the formulas are these

The − input is at 0 V, so input k drives Vk / Rk into it. No current enters the op-amp, so the sum flows through Rf, from the − node towards the output:

Vout = −Rf × (V1 / R1 + V2 / R2 + …)

The feedback network divides the output by 1 + Rf / (R1 ∥ R2 ∥ …) on its way back to the − input, which equals 1 + Rf/R1 + Rf/R2 + …. That noise gain sets the bandwidth: GBW / (1 + Rf/R1 + Rf/R2 + …). Each input added lowers it.

Assumptions and limits

  • An ideal op-amp for the sum.
  • A symmetric supply, with the same headroom on both sides.
  • Each source is taken as having no resistance of its own. A source's resistance adds to its input resistor and lowers its weight.
  • Up to four inputs are offered, which is what still fits above the tab bar. More work the same way, each adding its own V / R term.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Non-inverting summing, with the inputs on the + side, is not covered.
  • Subtracting belongs to the Differential tool.

How it was checked

All on ±12 V with 1.5 V headroom and a 1 MHz GBW: - 10 kΩ all round, 1 V + 2 V: - −3 V, weights −1 and −1, 300 µA through Rf; - bandwidth 333.3 kHz (1 MHz / 3). - + add, with a third input of 1 V through 10 kΩ: −4 V, 250 kHz. - Three-channel mixer, R3 = 20 kΩ, 0.5 V on each input: −1.25 V, weight −0.5 on V3, 285.7 kHz. - Averager, Rf = 5 kΩ: −1.5 V. - 3-bit DAC, 10 / 20 / 40 kΩ, code 101 (5 V, 0 V, 5 V): −6.25 V. - 6 V + 6 V: the ideal −12 V clips at −10.5 V.

The review made these changes: - It moved clipping from the full supply to the supply less the headroom, and added the bandwidth. - It put Vout first and large, replacing a row of six small cells. - It limited the units to real ones and remembers them. - It rewrote the subtitle and note in plain words, and added examples. - The tool was renamed Summing, on Pierre's request. - Also on Pierre's request, inputs can be added, up to four. Each is one compact line with its weight, and the drawing grows one arm per input.

Active & semiconductor devices › Op-amps

Differential

(formerly Differential amplifier)

What it computes

For the one-op-amp difference amplifier, it gives: - the output for two input voltages; - the gain; - the common-mode rejection (CMRR), both as drawn and at worst with real resistors of a chosen tolerance; - the bandwidth; - where the output clips.

When the two arms are not balanced, it also gives how much of the output is leaked common-mode voltage.

Source

No standard applies. The output follows from the ideal op-amp model by superposition. The worst-case CMRR with resistor tolerance is derived below from the same equation. The headroom and gain-bandwidth figures come from the TL072, LM358 and MCP6002 datasheets, as listed in the Inverting section.

What it means

A difference amplifier outputs the difference between its inputs, V2 − V1, times a gain, and ignores the voltage both inputs share.

  • Common-mode voltage — the shared part, (V1 + V2) / 2. It is often much larger than the difference:
  • a sensor bridge sitting at 2.5 V with millivolts between its sides;
  • a current shunt at 12 V;
  • hum picked up equally on both wires.
  • Balanced arms — the circuit rejects the shared part only when R3 / R2 equals Rf / R1. The gain is then Rf / R1.
  • CMRR (common-mode rejection ratio) — how much more the difference is amplified than the shared voltage, in dB. With exactly matched resistors it is infinite.
  • CMRR with tolerance — real resistors are off by their tolerance. At worst, four ±1 % resistors at gain 1 leave only about 34 dB: a shared 12 V would still put about 240 mV on the output. That is why precision resistors, or a ready-made difference-amplifier chip with laser-trimmed resistors, are used.
  • Input loading — V1 sees R1 to the virtual input, and V2 sees R2 + R3 to ground. Both draw current from their sources, unlike an instrumentation amplifier.
  • Headroom and bandwidth — as on the other op-amp tools. The bandwidth is GBW / (1 + Rf / R1).

The headroom and GBW are remembered for all the op-amp tools.

Why the formulas are these

With k = Rf / R1 and β = R3 / (R2 + R3), the + input sits at β × V2, and the op-amp holds the − input there too. So

Vout = β(1 + k) × V2 − k × V1

Writing V1 and V2 as the common part Vcm plus or minus half the difference Vd gives

Vout = [β(1 + k) + k] / 2 × Vd + [β(1 + k) − k] × Vcm
     =        Ad        × Vd +       Acm        × Vcm

Acm is zero exactly when β(1 + k) = k, which means R3 / R2 = Rf / R1. Then Ad = k.

Worst case with tolerance. Let the ratios Rf / R1 and R3 / R2 be off by fractions a and b. To first order, Acm = k(b − a) / (1 + k). Each ratio of two ±t resistors can be off by 2t, in opposite directions, so at worst |Acm| = 4tk / (1 + k). With Ad ≈ k:

CMRR (worst) = (1 + Rf / R1) / 4t

A higher gain helps: the same ±1 % resistors give about 49 dB at gain 10.

Assumptions and limits

  • An ideal op-amp. The op-amp's own CMRR, usually 70–100 dB, is assumed far better than the resistors'. With 0.1 % resistors at high gain, the two become comparable.
  • Ideal sources. Each source is taken as having no resistance of its own. A source's resistance adds to R1 or R2 and unbalances the arms.
  • Inputs within range. The op-amp's inputs sit at β × V2, which must stay within its input range even when V1 and V2 are higher. In the 12 V shunt example they sit at about 6 V.
  • Symmetric supply, with the same headroom on both sides.

What it deliberately does not do

  • The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier, with high input impedance, is not covered.
  • Frequency-dependent CMRR is not calculated.

How it was checked

  • Four 10 kΩ, 1 V and 1.1 V: 100 mV out, CMRR ∞ as drawn, 34 dB at ±1 %, 500 kHz on a 1 MHz op-amp.
  • Bridge at 2.5 V, 10 k / 100 k: 2.49 V and 2.51 V give 200 mV, gain 10, 48.8 dB at ±1 %, 90.91 kHz.
  • R3 = 110 kΩ instead of 100 kΩ:
  • 409.2 mV out;
  • CMRR 41.6 dB;
  • 50.9 % of the output is leaked common-mode voltage.
  • Shunt at 12 V (11.9 V and 12 V): 100 mV out, common-mode voltage 11.95 V.
  • ±0.1 % at gain 1: 54 dB.

These figures were checked in a separate calculation.

The review made these changes: - It moved clipping from the full supply to the supply less the headroom, and added the bandwidth. - It added the worst-case CMRR for a chosen resistor tolerance. - It put Vout first and large, replacing a row of six small cells. - It removed the waveform. That waveform showed an invented slow interference unrelated to the entered inputs. - It limited the units to real ones and remembers them. - It rewrote the note in plain words and added examples. - The tool was renamed Differential, on Pierre's request.

Active & semiconductor devices › Optoelectronics

Photocell / LDR

What it computes

For a light-dependent resistor in a voltage divider with a fixed resistor, it gives: - the output voltage at a given light level; - the LDR's resistance at that light; - the range of output the part's 2:1 manufacturing spread can give; - how much the output changes for each ×10 of light; - the fixed resistor that would make the divider most sensitive; - the current drawn.

It plots the output across four decades of light.

Source

GL55-series data from the series' datasheet, "GL55 Series CdS Photoresistor Manual" (5 pages; the copy read names no manufacturer). - Test conditions — light resistance is measured at 10 lx under standard light source A (2856 K), after two hours at 400–600 lx. - γ — defined as lg(R10 / R100), the logarithm of the ratio of the resistances at 10 and 100 lx.

Part R at 10 lx Dark resistance (min) γ Rise / fall
GL5516 5–10 kΩ 0.5 MΩ 0.5 30 / 30 ms
GL5528 10–20 kΩ 1 MΩ 0.6 20 / 30 ms
GL5537-1 20–30 kΩ 2 MΩ 0.6 20 / 30 ms
GL5537-2 30–50 kΩ 3 MΩ 0.7 20 / 30 ms
GL5539 50–100 kΩ 5 MΩ 0.8 20 / 30 ms
GL5549 100–200 kΩ 10 MΩ 0.9 20 / 30 ms

Other vendors' sheets for the same names differ a little. One gives 8–20 kΩ for the GL5528, for example, so the spread is real.

What it means

An LDR (light-dependent resistor, photoresistor or photocell) is a resistor whose value falls as the light rises. It is thousands of ohms in a dim room, a few hundred in daylight, and megohms in the dark. The common ones are made of cadmium sulphide (CdS).

  • Lux (lx) — the unit of illuminance, how much light falls on a surface. Rough values:
  • about 1 lx at deep twilight;
  • 50–100 lx in a dim room;
  • 300–500 lx in an office;
  • 10 000 lx and more in daylight.
  • R at 10 lx — the datasheet's reference resistance.
  • γ — how steeply the resistance falls: each ×10 of light divides it by 10^γ. With γ = 0.6, 100 lx gives about a quarter of the 10 lx value.
  • The divider — the LDR and a fixed resistor R between the supply and ground. The midpoint, Vout, follows the light:
  • with the LDR on top, brighter light gives a higher Vout;
  • with it at the bottom, darker gives a higher Vout, as for a night light that switches on at dusk.
  • Sensitivity — the change of Vout for each ×10 of light. It is largest when R equals the LDR's resistance at the light level you care about, which puts Vout at half the supply. "Best R here" gives that value.
  • Spread — pieces of the same part differ by up to 2:1 at 10 lx. With a part chosen, the tool shows the range of Vout this gives, and draws it as two faint curves.

Choosing a part fills in its middle R at 10 lx and its γ. Typing your own values switches the choice to Custom.

Why the formulas are these

The datasheet's γ = lg(R10 / R100) describes a straight line of slope −γ on log-log axes, so

R_LDR = R(10 lx) × (light / 10)^−γ

The divider gives Vout = Vcc × R / (R_LDR + R) with the LDR on top, or Vcc × R_LDR / (R_LDR + R) with it at the bottom.

Differentiating with respect to log₁₀ of the light gives

± ln 10 × γ × Vcc × R × R_LDR / (R_LDR + R)²

per ×10 of light. Setting its derivative with respect to R to zero gives R = R_LDR.

Assumptions and limits

  • The power law is a straight-line fit through the datasheet's two defining points, 10 lx and 100 lx. It is least reliable far from them. Below about 1 lx the cell heads towards its dark resistance instead, and the tool warns. The dark resistance is measured 10 s after the light is switched off, so the cell also recovers slowly.
  • Slow. CdS cells take tens of milliseconds to respond (20–30 ms here), so they suit day/night switching, not fast signals.
  • Temperature and history. The resistance also drifts with temperature and with recent exposure. An LDR is not a precision light meter.
  • Light source. The values are for an incandescent-like source (2856 K). LEDs and daylight have different spectra, and the cell peaks at 540 nm (green).
  • No loading — the circuit reading Vout is assumed to draw no current.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Photodiodes and phototransistors, which are faster and linear, are not covered.
  • Switching thresholds with hysteresis belong to the Comparators tool.

How it was checked

All at 5 V, with the GL5528's middle value, 15 kΩ at 10 lx, γ 0.6: - On top, 100 lx, R = 10 kΩ: - LDR 3.768 kΩ, Vout 3.632 V; - 3.33–4 V across the 10–20 kΩ spread; - +1.373 V per ×10 of light, 363.2 µA. - At the bottom, 10 lx, R = 15 kΩ: exactly 2.5 V. - 300 lx: 1.949 kΩ, and 2.532 V with R = 2 kΩ. - GL5516 at 10 000 lx: 237.2 Ω, and 4.884 V with R = 10 kΩ.

The review made these changes: - It added the GL55 parts from their datasheet, with the spread shown in the result and on the curve. - It added the choice of LDR on top or at the bottom. - It put Vout first and large. - It enlarged the curve's 8 px labels to 11 px. - It limited the units to real ones and remembers them. - It rewrote the note in plain words, with typical light levels, and added the warning below 1 lx and examples.

Active & semiconductor devices › Optoelectronics

Optocoupler

What it computes

For a phototransistor optocoupler driven through a resistor, with a pull-up on the output side: - the input resistor Rin for the LED current wanted, the nearest E24 value, and the power in it; - the collector current the minimum CTR makes available; - the current the pull-up needs to pull the output low; - the output voltage with the LED on; - whether the output really pulls low, and with how much margin.

Source

Data read from the manufacturers' datasheets themselves.

Sharp PC817X series (sheet D2-A03101EN, 2003): - CTR by rank — measured at IF = 5 mA, VCE = 5 V, from the collector-current bins:

Rank CTR
A 80–160 %
B 130–260 %
C 200–400 %
D 300–600 %
Unranked 50–600 %
  • VF — 1.2 V typical, 1.4 V maximum, at 20 mA.
  • VCE(sat) — 0.1 V typical, 0.2 V maximum, at IF = 20 mA, IC = 1 mA.
  • Rise / fall time — 4 / 3 µs typical (VCE 2 V, IC 2 mA, RL 100 Ω).

Vishay 4N35 (document 81181, rev. 1.2, 2010): - CTR — at least 100 % at IF = 10 mA, VCE = 10 V. Over −55 to +100 °C it is at least 40 %, 50 % typical. - VF — 1.3 V typical, 1.5 V maximum, at 10 mA. - Switching time — 10 µs typical (VCC 10 V, IC 2 mA, RL 100 Ω). - VCE(sat) — no limit is given. Its curves of saturated CTR are drawn at VCE = 0.4 V, which the tool uses.

What it means

An optocoupler is an LED and a light-sensitive transistor sealed in one package, facing each other across an insulating gap. The signal crosses as light, so the two circuits share no wire. They can sit at very different voltages, a microcontroller and mains equipment for example; the PC817 and 4N35 are both rated for 5 kV rms between their sides.

  • Rin — sets the LED current If, as for any LED: Rin = (Vin − Vf) / If.
  • CTR (current transfer ratio) — the collector current the transistor can pass for a given LED current, in %. A CTR of 50 % turns 10 mA of LED current into 5 mA available on the output side.
  • Pull-up RL — from Vcc to the transistor's collector:
  • with the LED off, the output reads high;
  • with it on, the transistor pulls the output low, provided it can pass the current RL needs: (Vcc − Vce(sat)) / RL.
  • Vce(sat) — the voltage left across the transistor when it is fully on: 0.2 V for the PC817.
  • Margin — CTR varies widely between pieces, which is why the PC817 is sold in ranks. It is also lower when the transistor is saturated, and it falls as the LED ages and with temperature.
  • Design on the minimum CTR, and aim for about 2× the current RL needs. That 2× is a rule of thumb, not a datasheet figure.
  • Below 1× the output stops part way down, between logic levels.

Choosing a part fills in its minimum CTR, Vf and Vce(sat). Typing your own values switches it to Custom.

Why the formulas are these

Rin = (Vin − Vf) / If
Ic available = If × CTR / 100
Ic needed = (Vcc − Vce(sat)) / RL

If Ic available ≥ Ic needed, the transistor saturates and Vout = Vce(sat). Otherwise it passes only Ic available, and Vout = Vcc − Ic available × RL.

Assumptions and limits

  • CTR at the test current. CTR changes with If; both datasheets plot it against If. The ranks are specified at 5 mA (PC817) and 10 mA (4N35), so far from those currents read the curve.
  • Speed. Phototransistor optocouplers are slow, a few microseconds, and a larger RL makes them slower. Fast signals need a logic-output part.
  • The input source is taken as ideal, and the LED is driven with steady DC.
  • No load on Vout other than RL.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Switching speed is not calculated.
  • Triac-output and logic-output optocouplers are not covered.

How it was checked

  • PC817, any rank, 5 V, 10 mA, 10 kΩ to 5 V:
  • Rin 380 Ω, nearest E24 390 Ω giving 9.744 mA, 38 mW;
  • 5 mA available, 480 µA needed: 10× margin, Vout 200 mV.
  • 3.3 V drive at 5 mA: 420 Ω, 5.2× margin.
  • 1 kΩ to 12 V with 2 mA: needs 11.8 mA but only 1 mA is available, so the output stops at 11 V.
  • 4N35 at 10 mA from 5 V: 370 Ω, nearest E24 360 Ω, Vout 400 mV.
  • 1 mA at 50 %: only 1× over, so the tool flags it.

The review made these changes: - The output check used a fixed 0.3 V saturation. It now takes the part's datasheet Vce(sat) and minimum CTR, from a choice of PC817 ranks or the 4N35. - It added the 2× margin advice. - It put Rin first and large, and draws it green as the calculated part. - It added the nearest E24 value. - It limited the units to real ones, rewrote the note in plain words and added examples.

Wavelength ↔ color

(formerly Light wavelength ↔ color)

What it computes

For a wavelength from 200 nm to 1100 nm, it gives: - the colour name, with a swatch; - the named region it falls in (ultraviolet, visible or infrared, and which part of them); - the energy of one photon, in electron-volts; - the frequency.

It marks the wavelength on a drawn spectrum.

Source

  • Region limits — the UV divisions follow ISO 20473:2007, for optics and photonics: UV-A 315–380 nm, UV-B 280–315 nm, UV-C 100–280 nm. The visible band is 380–780 nm, and IR-A is 780–1400 nm and IR-B 1400–3000 nm, as the CIE defines them.
  • These limits were read from Opsytec's published table of spectral ranges by standard (2024), not from the standards themselves.
  • The CIE notes that visible light has no precise limits: the lower one lies between 360 and 400 nm, the upper one between 760 and 830 nm.
  • Colour names — no standard names the colours inside the visible band. Published tables disagree by 10–20 nm, and some add cyan or indigo. The tool uses one common set: violet from 380 nm, blue 450, green 495, yellow 570, orange 590, red 620 to 780.
  • The examples' LEDs — taken from their datasheets: Kingbright WP7113SRC/DU, WP7113ZGC and WP7113QBC/D, and Vishay TSAL6200.
  • The swatch — drawn with Dan Bruton's wavelength-to-RGB approximation, a way to put a colour on screen. It is not colorimetry.

What it means

  • Wavelength — light is an electromagnetic wave, and its wavelength λ, in nanometres (millionths of a millimetre), sets its colour. The eye sees about 380 nm (violet) to 780 nm (red).
  • Shorter than that is ultraviolet: UV-A, then UV-B, then UV-C.
  • Longer is infrared: IR-A is the near infrared that remote controls and optocouplers use.
  • Photon energy — light comes in packets, photons, each carrying an energy E = 1239.84 / λ electron-volts (eV). Blue photons carry more than red.
  • LEDs — an LED makes photons of roughly its material's energy, so its forward voltage tracks its colour:
  • red, yellow and infrared LEDs run at about the photon energy: a 640 nm red, at 1.94 eV, needs 1.85 V;
  • blue and true-green LEDs need about 3.3 V, well above it.
  • Dominant and peak wavelength — an LED datasheet gives both. The dominant wavelength is the colour the eye sees; the peak is where the LED emits most. Names follow the dominant one.
  • Naming varies — Kingbright sells its WP7113ID, at 617 nm, as "High Efficiency Red", yet 617 nm is orange in the set used here.

Why the formulas are these

f = c / λ,   E = h × f = h × c / λ

With h × c = 1239.84 eV·nm, E in eV is 1239.84 divided by λ in nm. With c = 299 792 458 m/s, 525 nm is 571 THz.

Assumptions and limits

  • Single wavelengths. Real sources emit a band. LEDs are 20–45 nm wide (half-width, from the same datasheets), and white light mixes many wavelengths.
  • Approximate swatch. Screens cannot show pure spectral colours. The swatch is an approximation, and blank outside 380–780 nm.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Colour mixing and colour spaces (RGB, CIE xy) are not covered.
  • The eye's sensitivity (lumens) is not calculated.

How it was checked

  • 525 nm: green, visible, 2.362 eV, 571 THz.
  • Red LED at 640 nm: red, 1.937 eV.
  • 617 nm: orange in this set, 2.009 eV.
  • IR LED at 940 nm: infrared, IR-A, 1.319 eV.
  • 760 nm: still red, since visible light runs to 780 nm.
  • 365 nm: ultraviolet, UV-A.

The review made these changes: - Infrared started at 750 nm; it now starts at 780 nm, the limit ISO 20473 and the CIE use. - It added the named UV and IR regions. - It removed a source attribution ("Britannica") that had never been checked. - It corrected the claim that photon energy is the floor of an LED's forward voltage: a red LED runs slightly below it. - It put the colour first and large, with its swatch. - It enlarged the strip's 9 px labels to 11 px. - It added LED examples from datasheets and rewrote the note in plain words. - It shortened the name to Wavelength ↔ color, which fits on the phone.

Digital & logic circuits › Logic gates

Logic gates

(formerly Basic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR))

What it computes

For each of the seven basic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR), it shows: - the gate's symbol; - its truth table; - its Boolean expression; - the same operation written in code; - a common chip that contains it.

Tap a row of the truth table to set the inputs. The symbol then shows the levels on its wires, and the output Y appears large.

Source

  • Symbols — these are the "distinctive shape" symbols: a D for AND, a shield for OR, a triangle for NOT. Wikipedia's "Logic gate" article says ANSI/IEEE Std 91-1984 (and its supplement 91a-1991) defines both these and the rectangular IEC-style symbols, and that the distinctive shapes come from MIL-STD-806. The standard itself was not read. The app uses the distinctive shapes throughout, as it uses zigzag resistors.
  • Chips — Texas Instruments' product pages confirm the SN74HC00 (four NAND gates), SN74HC04 (six inverters), SN74HC08 (four AND) and SN74HC32 (four OR), all for 2–6 V. Distributor listings of TI parts confirm the 74HC02 (four NOR) and 74HC86 (four XOR).
  • The 74HC7266 (four XNOR) is in a Philips/Nexperia datasheet listed by a distributor. TI's own version is obsolete.

What it means

A logic gate works on two levels, 0 and 1. In a 5 V circuit these are a voltage near 0 V and one near 5 V. The truth table lists every combination of inputs and the output each gives. A bar over an expression means "inverted".

Gate Output is 1 when… Expression In C / Python
AND A and B are both 1 Y = A · B a & b
OR A or B, or both, is 1 Y = A + B a | b
NOT A is 0 (it inverts) Y = Ā !a / not a
NAND not both are 1 Y = (A · B)‾ !(a & b) / not (a & b)
NOR both are 0 Y = (A + B)‾ !(a | b) / not (a | b)
XOR A and B differ Y = A ⊕ B a ^ b
XNOR A and B are the same Y = (A ⊕ B)‾ !(a ^ b) / not (a ^ b)
  • NAND and NOR are universal — any logic, however complex, can be built from either one alone. A NAND with its inputs tied together is a NOT.
  • XOR and AND add two bits — XOR gives the sum and AND the carry, which makes a half adder.
  • Unused inputs — on CMOS chips such as the 74HC series, an input left floating can make the gate switch at random and draw extra current. Tie every unused input to 0 V or to the supply.

Why the formulas are these

Each truth table is computed from the gate's function, so a row cannot disagree with the symbol. The code forms use the bitwise operators on the values 0 and 1. In Python, not returns True or False rather than 1 or 0.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal logic levels. Real gates have input thresholds, output drive limits and a propagation delay, given on each chip's datasheet. They are not modelled.
  • Two-input versions. Chips with three or more inputs per gate exist (for example triple 3-input AND); the logic extends the same way.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Simplifying a larger expression belongs to Karnaugh map simplification.
  • Flip-flops, which remember, have their own tool.

How it was checked

  • AND: with A = 1, B = 1, Y = 1; tapping the 0 1 row gives 0.
  • XOR: 1 0 gives 1, and 1 1 gives 0, the sum bit of a half adder.
  • NOT: A = 1 gives Y = 0.
  • NAND: with both inputs at 1, Y = 0 (the NOT example).
  • Remembered: the chosen gate comes back when the tool reopens.

The review made these changes: - It corrected the standard cited ("ANSI/IEEE 315") to IEEE Std 91. - It made the truth table tappable, with the levels shown on the symbol and Y large. - For each gate, it added the description in plain words, the code form and a common 74HC chip, with the CMOS unused-input advice. - It added examples and remembers the chosen gate. - The tool was renamed Logic gates, on Pierre's choice, to fit on one line.

Digital & logic circuits › Logic gates

Karnaugh map

(formerly Karnaugh map simplification)

What it computes

Takes a truth table for 2, 3 or 4 variables, where each cell is 0, 1 or a don't-care. It returns: - the minimum sum-of-products expression, with each product term drawn as a group on the map in its own colour; - the minimum product of sums, under the expression; - the exclusive-OR form, when the function is a parity.

Tap a cell to cycle it through 0, 1 and X. The number of variables is remembered, and four examples in the bulb load ready-made maps.

Plain words: - Cell — one combination of the inputs. Its small number is the binary value of A B C D, and it holds the output. - Minterm — a cell that is 1. - Literal — one letter in a term, plain or barred. A bar means the inverted variable. - Sum of products — terms ANDed, then ORed together. - Product of sums — ORs ANDed together. - Don't-care (X) — an input combination that never happens, so its output may be whatever helps.

Source

The map is Karnaugh's (1953), itself a reworking of the Veitch diagram. The minimisation is Quine–McCluskey, which is an exact algorithm rather than a heuristic; the covering step is solved by exhaustive search, which is affordable at four variables and would not be at twenty.

Why the formulas are these

The whole method rests on the ordering along the edges: 00, 01, 11, 10, not 00, 01, 10, 11. That is Gray code, and it means any two side-by-side cells differ in exactly one variable. When two adjacent cells are both 1, that variable appears once true and once complemented, so it cancels:

A·B̄·C + A·B·C = A·C·(B̄ + B) = A·C

Extend it and a rectangle of 2^k cells cancels k variables. A pair drops one, a block of four drops two, eight drops three. That is the entire trick — the map is just an arrangement that puts algebraically adjacent terms physically next to each other.

The edges wrap. The first and last columns also differ in one variable (00 and 10 differ only in the middle bit), and so do the first and last rows. The map is really a torus. That is why the four corners of a four-variable map form one group of four, and why a group can run off one edge and continue on the other. A torus rectangle has no single box on a flat sheet, so the tool draws wrapping groups as two or four pieces in the same colour.

Quine–McCluskey. Terms are combined pairwise wherever they differ in one bit, the shared bit becoming a dash; repeat until nothing more combines. What never combined is a prime implicant — a group that cannot be made larger. Then a cover must be chosen: a minterm covered by exactly one prime implicant forces that implicant in (it is essential), and the rest is a set-cover problem solved here by branch and bound.

The cover is ordered fewest terms first, then fewest literals. The second key matters: several covers can tie on term count while differing in how many variables survive, and the answer a textbook prints is the one with fewer letters.

Don't-cares are included when forming groups but never required to be covered. That is where most of the saving usually comes from: an X adjacent to a group lets the group double in size, dropping another variable for free.

Parity is what the map cannot see. A checkerboard of ones has no two adjacent cells, so every group is a single cell and the sum of products comes out at full length — twelve of twelve literals on a three-variable map, nothing saved at all. That function is exclusive-OR:

A ⊕ B ⊕ C = 1 whenever an odd number of A, B, C are 1

Two XOR gates implement it against four ANDs and an OR for the sum of products. The map cannot find this because XOR is not a sum of products in any small form — its minimal SOP genuinely is the long one. The tool therefore tests, separately from the map, whether the function is the parity of any subset of its variables (or the complement of one) and prints that form when it is.

Assumptions and limits

  • Two to four variables. Five and six variable maps exist, drawn as stacked pairs, but they stop being readable and the whole point of the map is that you can see it.
  • The result is a minimum, not the minimum: several different expressions can tie on both term and literal count, and the tool shows one of them.
  • Literal count is a proxy for cost, not a gate count. It ignores that inverters may be free if a signal is already available complemented, and that fan-in is limited in real logic families.
  • No account of hazards. A minimal cover can contain a static hazard — a glitch when two inputs change at once — which is removed by adding a redundant group that the minimiser will never choose because it costs a term.

What it deliberately does not do

  • More than four variables, as above.
  • Hazard-free covers. Adding the redundant terms is a different objective from minimisation and would make the answers disagree with what a textbook shows.

How it was checked

A second minimiser was written independently for the purpose: enumerate every possible cube, discard those covering a zero, and find the smallest cover by iterative deepening. The two were compared over 3500 random functions at 2, 3 and 4 variables, and 12000 more were checked only for the expression reproducing the truth table at every care position.

That comparison earned its keep. Term counts matched from the start, but 34 of the first 3400 came back with more literals than the reference — the cover search was returning whichever minimum-size cover it reached first, with no tie-break on literals. A correct minimum by term count, and still not the printed answer.

The parity detector was checked exhaustively over all 256 three-variable functions: exactly eight are parity forms (three pairs and one triple, each with its complement), and each one's exclusive-OR form reproduces its truth table.

The product of sums (added in the 2026 review) is the same exact minimisation run on the zeros, keeping the same don't-cares. De Morgan's law then turns each group of zeros into a sum of inverted letters:

F̄ = A̅B̅ + …   →   F = (A + B)(…)

It was checked in the browser over 6000 random functions of 2 to 4 variables, with don't-cares. At all 47,615 positions that are not don't-cares, the product of sums reproduced the truth table.

The examples: - Majority of three — AB + AC + BC, with the product of sums (A + B)(A + C)(B + C). - BCD digit 5 or more — with codes 10–15 as don't-cares, A + BC + BD. - 4-input parity — eight terms of four letters, and A ⊕ B ⊕ C ⊕ D. - The four corners — they wrap around into the single term B̄D̄.

The review made these changes: - It added the product of sums, which an earlier version left out as not worth a second screen. It needs only one line. - It put the answer first and large. - It moved the cells' numbers above the group outlines, at 11 px. - It added plain definitions, examples, and remembers the number of variables. - The tool was renamed Karnaugh map, on Pierre's choice, to fit beside the bulb.

Digital & logic circuits › Sequential logic

Flip-flops

(formerly Flip-flops (SR, D, JK, T))

What it computes

For the four flip-flop types (SR, D, JK and T), it shows: - the symbol; - the truth table: what the next clock edge does in each input case; - the characteristic equation; - an eight-clock timing diagram, with the output Q computed by running the inputs through the flip-flop.

Tap an input at any clock in the timing diagram to flip it, and Q is recomputed. "Reset inputs" brings back the demonstration sequence. The chosen type is remembered.

Source

The behaviour of each type is textbook logic. The chips and timing figures were read from manufacturers' documents: - Nexperia 74HC74 (rev. 9, 2 April 2024): - a dual D flip-flop, triggered on the rising clock edge, with asynchronous active-low set and reset; - at 4.5 V and 25 °C, D must be steady at least 15 ns before the edge (setup) and 3 ns after it (hold); - the clock runs up to at least 24 MHz. - Nexperia 74HC112 — a dual JK flip-flop, triggered on the falling edge, with set and reset. - ST M74HC279 — four SR latches, with no clock.

What it means

A flip-flop stores one bit, Q; Q̄ is its opposite. It changes only at the clock's active edge, here the rising edge, and holds still in between. That is what lets many of them, such as the bits of a register or a counter, change in step. Q⁺ is the state after the next edge.

  • SR (set / reset):
  • S = 1 sets Q to 1, R = 1 resets it to 0, and both at 0 holds it;
  • S = R = 1 is forbidden: both outputs are driven the same way, and when the inputs are released together the state is unpredictable. The timing diagram draws that unknown stretch dashed with a "?", until the next set or reset defines Q again;
  • on its own, without a clock, the circuit is an SR latch.
  • D (data) — Q takes the value D had at the edge and ignores D in between. One D flip-flop is one bit of a register.
  • JK — like SR, but J = K = 1 toggles Q instead of being forbidden. It is the general-purpose type: D and T are both a JK with its inputs tied.
  • T (toggle) — T = 1 flips Q at every edge, so Q is a square wave at half the clock frequency, with a 50 % duty cycle whatever the clock's.
  • Chained, n stages divide by 2ⁿ: a ripple counter.
  • It is built from a JK with J and K tied high, or a D with Q̄ fed back to D.
  • Setup and hold — the inputs must be steady for a short time before and after the edge, or the result is not guaranteed. A datasheet gives both, as above for the 74HC74.

Why the formulas are these

The characteristic equations follow from the truth tables:

SR:  Q⁺ = S + R̄ · Q        (with S · R = 0)
D:   Q⁺ = D
JK:  Q⁺ = J · Q̄ + K̄ · Q
T:   Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q

In the timing diagram, each input holds across a whole clock cycle, and Q updates on the rising edge that ends it. Q starts at 0. After SR's forbidden input, Q is unknown. A hold or toggle keeps an unknown unknown, and only a set or reset ends it.

Assumptions and limits

  • One edge for all four. All four types are drawn edge-triggered on the rising edge. Some chips act on the falling edge (74HC112), and latches are level-sensitive instead.
  • Ideal timing. Propagation delay, setup and hold violations and metastability are not simulated; the inputs are taken as meeting the setup and hold times.
  • No set or reset pins. The asynchronous set and reset inputs of real chips are not drawn.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Counters and shift registers built from several flip-flops are not simulated.

How it was checked

  • D, demonstration inputs: Q runs 0 0 1 1 0 1 0 0.
  • Tapping D high at the first clock makes it 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 0, and "Reset inputs" restores it.
  • T held at 1: 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1, half the clock frequency.
  • SR with set, hold, S = R = 1, two holds, reset, hold: 0 1 1 ? ? ? 0 0. Q is unknown from the forbidden input until the reset.

The review made these changes: - It fixed the forbidden SR input. The old diagram quietly kept Q unchanged, as if the state were known; it now shows it unknown until the next set or reset. - It made the inputs tappable, with a reset. - It enlarged the 10 px labels to 11 px. - It added setup and hold times and the chips from Nexperia and ST documents. - It added plain-word explanations and examples, and remembers the type. - The tool was renamed Flip-flops, on Pierre's choice, to fit beside the bulb.

Digital & logic circuits › Sequential logic

Multivibrators

(formerly Multivibrators (astable/monostable))

What it computes

For the classic two-transistor multivibrator, the tool works in two modes.

Astable (free-running): - the frequency and duty cycle from the two resistor–capacitor pairs, or the resistors from a frequency and duty you type; - the period and its two halves; - the same circuit in standard E-series values, with a suggested collector resistor.

Monostable (one-shot): - the pulse width from R and C, or R from the width you type; - the capacitor's recovery time; - the shortest time between triggers and the highest trigger rate; - the E-series value of R.

Every field works in both directions, and the timing diagrams are drawn to the computed times.

Source

  • The timing is the standard textbook analysis of the circuit. Each half-cycle is one RC time constant times ln 2, about 0.693 RC, with Vbe and Vce(sat) neglected as the references do.
  • The emitter–base limit is read from the datasheets: VEBO is 6 V for a 2N3904 (Diodes Inc. MMBT3904, DS30036) and a BC547 (Fairchild, rev. A2), and 5 V for the BC548–BC550 (same Fairchild sheet).

What it means

A multivibrator is two transistors that switch each other on and off through capacitors.

  • Astable — it has no stable state, so it oscillates by itself: an LED flasher, a tone.
  • Monostable — it has one stable state. A trigger flips it for one timed pulse, and it returns by itself: a one-shot.
  • T1 and T2 — the two halves of the astable's cycle, set by R1·C1 and R2·C2.
  • Duty — the share of the period spent in the first half, T1.
  • How a half-cycle works — when one transistor switches on, its collector drops and pulls the other transistor's base, through the coupling capacitor, to about −Vcc. That base then climbs back through its resistor toward +Vcc and switches on as it passes zero, after ln 2 × R × C. The supply voltage cancels out, so the frequency does not depend on it.
  • The catch with high supplies — the reversed base reaches about −Vcc. A small transistor's emitter–base junction withstands only 5–6 V in reverse (VEBO). On a higher supply it breaks down, and the circuit runs faster than the formula says.
  • The collector resistor Rc — squeezed from both sides:
  • at least R / β (β, or hFE, is the current gain), or the transistor stops switching fully on;
  • at most about R / 10, or the collector's rising edge softens.

The tool suggests R / 10 in your E-series. - Monostable recovery — after each pulse the capacitor must recharge through Rc, about 5 × Rc × C, before the next trigger does anything useful. Triggering faster gives short pulses, not more of them. The large result is that shortest interval. - Rb (monostable) only holds Q1's base low while Q2 is on. It sets no timing, so it is not calculated.

Why the formulas are these

T1 = ln 2 × R1 × C1,   T2 = ln 2 × R2 × C2
Frequency = 1 / (T1 + T2),   Duty = T1 / (T1 + T2)
Pulse width = ln 2 × R × C,   Recovery ≈ 5 × Rc × C
Shortest time between triggers = Pulse width + Recovery
  • ln 2 — a capacitor charging toward +Vcc from −Vcc crosses zero when half the 2·Vcc swing is done. That takes RC × ln 2.
  • Typing a frequency — scales both resistors and keeps the duty and the capacitors.
  • Typing a duty — shares the period between them and keeps the frequency.
  • The capacitors are never rewritten, since they are the part you have in the drawer.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal switches. Vbe and Vce(sat) are neglected. With them, the base starts at about Vbe − (Vcc − Vce(sat)) and switches on at Vbe rather than 0 V, so each half takes a little longer: about 0.72 RC instead of 0.693 RC on 9 V, and 0.74 RC on 5 V. The real frequency is therefore a few percent lower than calculated, more so on low supplies.
  • The 5 RC recovery is a rule of thumb (99 % recharged).
  • Capacitor tolerance, often ±20 % for electrolytics, matters more than the resistors' tolerance for the timing.

What it deliberately does not do

  • The 555 timer versions have their own tool.
  • Bistable multivibrators, which are flip-flops, have their own tool.

How it was checked

  • 47 k / 10 µF on both sides: period 651.6 ms (T1 = T2 = 325.8 ms), 1.535 Hz, Rc 4.7 kΩ suggested.
  • 68 k / 10 µF: 1.061 Hz.
  • 10 k and 100 k with 10 µF: T1 69.31 ms, T2 693.1 ms, duty 9.091 %.
  • 10 k / 68 nF: 1.061 kHz.
  • Monostable, 68 k / 10 µF with Rc 6.8 k:
  • pulse 471.3 ms;
  • recovery 340 ms;
  • shortest interval 811.3 ms, up to 1.233 Hz.
  • Typing 2 Hz: both 10 µF resistors become 36.067 kΩ.

The review made these changes: - It put the period, or the shortest trigger interval, first and large. - It limited the units to real ones (Ω–MΩ, pF–µF, µs–s). - It enlarged the timing labels to 11 px. - It added plain definitions, with the VEBO figures from datasheets. - It added examples, and remembers the mode and the tolerance. - The tool was renamed Multivibrators, on Pierre's choice.

555 timer

(formerly 555 Timer (astable/monostable))

What it computes

The tool covers the 555 timer chip in its two classic circuits.

Astable (free-running): - the frequency and duty cycle from R1, R2 and C, or the resistors from a frequency and duty you type; - the period, with its high and low times; - the two resistors in standard E-series values; - the trigger and threshold voltages, ⅓ and ⅔ of Vcc.

Monostable (one-shot): - the pulse width from R and C, or R from the width you type; - R in standard E-series values; - the trigger and threshold voltages.

Every field works in both directions. The timing diagram, with the capacitor's voltage above the output, is drawn to the computed times. The mode and the tolerance are remembered.

Source

Texas Instruments, NA555 / NE555 / SA555 / SE555 datasheet, SLFS022K (revised March 2026), was read for: - the formulas: - astable: tH ≈ 0.693 (RA + RB) C, tL ≈ 0.693 RB C, f ≈ 1.44 / ((RA + 2 RB) C), duty (RA + RB) / (RA + 2 RB); - monostable: tw ≈ 1.1 RA C.

RA and RB are R1 and R2 here. - the levels: trigger about ⅓ Vcc and threshold about ⅔ Vcc. At 5 V the trigger level is 1.1–2.2 V (1.67 V typical). - the supply: 4.5 to 16 V for the NE555. - the frequency: TI advises 100 kHz or below, to reduce distortion, and the CMOS TLC555 above that. - the pulse: the shortest monostable pulse is about 10 µs. - Trig must be back high at least 10 µs before the pulse ends, or the output stays high. - Retriggering cannot happen during the timing cycle. - the largest resistors: the threshold pin draws up to 250 nA (30 nA typical). TI gives the resulting limit as RA + RB ≈ 3.4 MΩ at 5 V and ≈ 10 MΩ at 15 V. - the smallest resistors: TI's timing figures and test circuits start at RA = 1 kΩ. No explicit minimum is stated. The discharge switch is specified at 0.4 V maximum while sinking 8 mA, at 5 V. - the pins: RESET is tied to Vcc when it is not used. The CONT pin may be decoupled with a capacitor, 0.01 µF in TI's figure.

What it means

A 555 is a timer chip, with two comparators, a latch and a discharge switch inside. The pins in the drawing are: - TRG, pin 2, the trigger: a voltage below ⅓ Vcc starts a high output; - THR, pin 6, the threshold: a voltage above ⅔ Vcc ends it; - DIS, pin 7, the discharge: shorted to ground while the output is low, which empties C; - CTL, pin 5, the control voltage: it sets the two levels, and 10 nF to ground keeps them steady; - pin 4, reset, tied to Vcc so it never resets.

The modes work like this: - Astable — C charges through R1 + R2 up to ⅔ Vcc. The output then goes low, and pin 7 drains C through R2 down to ⅓ Vcc, when the output goes high again. - Duty — the share of each period the output spends high. Since C charges through R1 + R2 but drains through R2 alone, the duty is always above 50 %. - Ask for 50 % or less, and a diode appears across R2 to take it out of the charge path. - Its forward drop is ignored, as datasheets ignore it, so the real duty is a little off. - Monostable — the output rests low, with C held empty. A trigger sends the output high, and C charges through R until it reaches ⅔ Vcc, which ends the pulse. - Vcc cancels out of every time, because both levels are fractions of it. It only sets the voltages you would probe and the resistor limits.

Why the formulas are these

Astable:    t high = ln 2 × (R1 + R2) × C    (with the diode: ln 2 × R1 × C)
            t low  = ln 2 × R2 × C
            Frequency = 1 / (t high + t low)
Monostable: Pulse width = ln 3 × R × C ≈ 1.1 × R × C
  • ln 2 — charging from ⅓ toward Vcc, C reaches ⅔ when half the remaining gap is closed, which takes RC × ln 2. Draining from ⅔ toward 0, it reaches ⅓ at half, again RC × ln 2.
  • ln 3 — the monostable starts from an empty C and must reach ⅔ of the way, leaving a third: RC × ln 3 = 1.0986 RC, TI's 1.1 RC.
  • The timing diagram uses the same curves, so they need no RC. Each stretch is drawn as 1 − ⅔ × 2^−s rising, ⅔ × 2^−s falling, and 1 − 3^−s for the monostable, where s runs from 0 to 1 across it.
  • Typing a frequency scales both resistors. Typing a duty redistributes them. C is never rewritten, since it is the part you have in the drawer.

Assumptions and limits

The tool cautions, without refusing, when: - R1 (or R) is under 1 kΩ, where TI's figures start. Pin 7 then sinks Vcc / R1 during every low time, or the whole time a monostable waits; the caution shows that current. - The charging resistance is too large. That is R1 + R2, R1 alone with the diode, or the monostable's R, against TI's limit: 3.4 MΩ at 5 V and 10 MΩ at 15 V, joined by a straight line. - The line keeps the charging current at the threshold around 500 nA, twice the pin's 250 nA maximum. - Applying it to the monostable's R is this tool's extension: TI states it for the astable, but it is the same pin sensing the same capacitor. - The frequency is over 100 kHz, or the pulse is under 10 µs. - Vcc is outside 4.5–16 V.

Beyond those: - The levels are typical. The real trigger and threshold levels spread, as above, so the real times do too. - Capacitor tolerance, often ±20 % for electrolytics, usually matters more than the resistors'. - The bipolar NE555 is modelled. CMOS versions such as the TLC555 use the same formulas, but have their own limits.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Two-transistor multivibrators have their own tool.
  • Switch debouncing has its own tool, Debounce / RC timing.

How it was checked

  • 4.7 k, 4.7 k, 100 nF: period 977.3 µs (1.023 kHz), duty 66.67 %, levels 1.667 V and 3.333 V at 5 V.
  • 10 k, 680 k, 1 µF: 949.6 ms (1.053 Hz), high 478.3 ms, duty 50.36 %.
  • 1 kHz at 50 % with 10 nF: the diode switches in, and R1 = R2 = 72.135 kΩ.
  • Monostable, 91 k and 100 µF: 9.997 s.
  • Monostable, 1 s with 100 nF: R = 9.1024 MΩ, cautioned at 5 V (over 3.4 MΩ), not at 15 V (under 10 MΩ).
  • R1 = 470 Ω at 5 V: the caution shows 10.6 mA into pin 7.

The review made these changes: - It put the period, or the pulse width, first and large. - It added the capacitor's voltage to the timing diagram. - It replaced the fixed 10 MΩ caution with TI's supply-dependent limit. The old wording claimed a 1 kΩ minimum "set by datasheets", which TI does not state, and the 1 kΩ caution now says what it rests on. - It added TI's 100 kHz, 10 µs and 4.5–16 V cautions. - It limited the units to real ones (Ω–MΩ, pF–µF, Hz–kHz, µs–s, Vcc in V). - It enlarged the 9–10 px labels to 11 px, and wrote the 10 nF out. - It added plain definitions of every pin, and examples. - It remembers the mode and the tolerance. - The tool was renamed 555 timer, on Pierre's choice.

Number bases

(formerly DEC / HEX / OCT / BIN conversion)

What it computes

One value, shown in decimal, hexadecimal, octal and binary at once. - Four live boxes. Type in any of them, and the other three follow. - A register width: 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits. - Unsigned or signed. Signed numbers are read as two's complement, the way processors store negative numbers: FFF6 in 16 bits is −10. - One button per bit. Each is numbered from bit 0 on the right, and tapping one flips it. The hex digit of each group of four bits sits under it.

The width and the signed choice are remembered.

Source

The arithmetic is standard: positional notation and two's complement. No datasheet is involved. The four widths are those of the usual fixed-size integer types (uint8 to uint64, int8 to int64).

What it means

  • A base is how many values one digit can take:
  • decimal, 10 (0–9);
  • hexadecimal, 16 (0–9, then A–F for 10–15);
  • octal, 8 (0–7);
  • binary, 2 (0 and 1).

Each place is worth the base times the place to its right. - A bit is one binary digit. Four bits are a nibble, which is exactly one hex digit, and eight bits are a byte: two hex digits. That is why registers and memory are written in hex. - Octal groups bits by three. It survives mostly in Unix file permissions (chmod 755), rarely in electronics. - Bit 0, on the right, is the least significant bit (LSB), worth 1. The top bit is the most significant (MSB). - Two's complement — in a signed number the top bit, the sign bit, counts −2ʷ⁻¹ instead of +2ʷ⁻¹, where w is the width. - All ones is therefore −1. - To negate a number, flip every bit and add 1. - Adding and subtracting work the same for signed and unsigned values, which is why processors use it.

Why the formulas are these

Value    = Σ digit × baseⁿ          (n = 0 at the right)
Unsigned:  0 … 2ʷ − 1
Signed:    −2ʷ⁻¹ … 2ʷ⁻¹ − 1,   value = bits − 2ʷ when the top bit is 1
  • One hex digit is four bits because 16 = 2⁴, and one octal digit is three bits because 8 = 2³. So hex and octal are read straight off the binary, four or three bits at a time.
  • A negative decimal is stored as 2ʷ plus the value: −10 in 16 bits is 65 536 − 10 = 65 526 = FFF6.

Assumptions and limits

  • Whole numbers only, up to 64 bits. Every value is an exact big integer, not a JavaScript number, so all 64 bits are exact. Typing more than 64 bits is refused, and the box goes back to the last value.
  • Widening. A value too big for the chosen width moves up to the next width that holds it (8 → 16 → 32 → 64). Choosing a wider width keeps the value, and a negative one is sign-extended (FFF6 → FFFFFFF6).
  • Narrowing. Choosing a narrower width keeps only the bits it can hold, as the register would, and the tool says so.
  • No padding. The boxes show no leading zeros, so 165 in 16 bits reads A5, not 00A5. The bit row shows every bit of the width.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Characters and their codes have their own tool, the ASCII table.
  • Fractions, floating point (IEEE 754), BCD and Gray code are not converted.

How it was checked

  • 165: A5, 245, 1010 0101.
  • FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF: 18446744073709551615 and 1777777777777777777777.
  • Before the review this came back as 10000000000000000 in hex, and as 18446744073709552000 in decimal.
  • JavaScript numbers hold integers exactly only up to 2⁵³.
  • 9007199254740993 (2⁵³ + 1): 20000000000001.
  • 300 typed at 8 bits widens to 16 bits: 12C, 0001 0010 1100.
  • Signed 8-bit FF: −1.
  • Signed 32-bit −1: FFFFFFFF, 37777777777.
  • Signed −10 at 8 bits, widened to 16: FFF6, still −10.
  • 1A5 narrowed to 8 bits: A5, with a note that the upper bits were dropped.
  • Examples:
  • 0x88 = 136 (bits 7 and 3);
  • FFF6 as int16 = −10;
  • FFFFFFFF = 4,294,967,295. As a 32-bit millisecond counter, that is 49.7 days before it wraps.

The review made these changes: - It fixed the conversion of values above 2⁵³, which were silently wrong. Values are now exact BigInts. - It replaced the base pills, the input and the four separate results with four live boxes. - It added the register width and signed (two's complement) reading, with a ± key for typing negatives. - It added the tappable bit row, with the hex digit under each nibble and the sign bit marked. - It added plain definitions, examples and remembered settings. - The tool was renamed Number bases, on Pierre's choice.

Digital & logic circuits › Number systems

ASCII table

What it computes

The 128 ASCII characters on one screen, as the classic chart of 8 columns by 16 rows. Tap a character, or type it in one of the three live boxes: - Char takes a character, or a control character's name (LF, ESC, XOFF, TAB, SP…); - Dec takes the decimal code, 0–127; - Hex takes the hex code, 00–7F.

The card shows, for the chosen character: - its name, with the standard mnemonic for a control character; - its codes in octal and in binary, the binary grouped as column and row; - the C escape (\n, \t, \0…) and the Ctrl key that sends it, where there is one; - in plain words, what a control character does, how a letter relates to its other case, or a digit to its value.

Source

RFC 20, ASCII format for Network Interchange (October 1969), was read for this. It is based on USAS X3.4-1968, the US standard ASCII, and gives: - the mnemonics and full names of the 33 control characters, NUL to US and DEL. Code 9 is HT, horizontal tabulation, so the tool no longer calls it TAB (it still finds it by that name); - the definitions behind each plain-word meaning; - the chart: bits b7–b5 give the column (0–7), and b4–b1 the row (0–15).

The modern uses are common knowledge, not from RFC 20: - C's escapes; - XON/XOFF serial flow control on DC1/DC3; - Ctrl+C sending ETX and Ctrl+D sending EOT in a terminal; - CR LF line endings; - ESC starting a terminal control sequence.

What it means

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) gives 128 characters a 7-bit code. - Codes 0–31 and 127 are control characters: commands for a terminal, printer or modem rather than symbols. RFC 20 groups some of them: - communication controls frame and acknowledge messages: SOH, STX, ETX, EOT, ENQ, ACK, NAK, SYN, ETB; - format effectors move the print position: BS, HT, LF, VT, FF, CR; - information separators split data, from the largest unit to the smallest: FS, GS, RS, US. - Codes 32–126 are printed characters. 32, the space, is a printed character that prints nothing. - Codes above 127 are not ASCII. Different 8-bit sets give them different characters (Latin-1, Windows-1252…). In UTF-8 they only appear inside multi-byte characters.

Uses worth knowing in electronics: - CR LF ends a line on Windows and on many serial devices. Linux and macOS end a line with LF alone. - XOFF (DC3) and XON (DC1) pause and resume a serial sender: software flow control, Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Q. - ESC [ starts a terminal control sequence, which sets colours and moves the cursor. - SOH, EOT, ACK, NAK and CAN run XMODEM, a simple serial file-transfer protocol.

Why the formulas are these

Hex code      = column digit, then row digit
Lower case    = upper case + 0x20        (bit 5)
Digit value   = code − 0x30              (48)
Ctrl + key    = key's code AND 0x1F      (bits 5 and 6 cleared)
  • The chart's columns are the top three bits and its rows the low four. A column is one hex digit, 0–7, and a row is the other, 0–F. So A, column 4 and row 1, is 0x41.
  • Letters were placed so the two cases differ in one bit. A to Z run 0x41–0x5A, and a to z run 0x61–0x7A: setting bit 5 lowers the case.
  • Digits were placed so the low four bits are the value. 0 to 9 run 0x30–0x39, so subtracting 0x30 (or masking with 0x0F) gives the number.
  • Ctrl clears bits 5 and 6. Ctrl+C is C (0x43) AND 0x1F, which is 3, ETX; Ctrl+[ is ESC.

Assumptions and limits

  • US ASCII only. The national variants of ISO 646 replace a few printed characters, such as # or [, and are not shown.
  • Uses, not rules. The modern uses in the card say what a code usually does today. A particular device may assign its own meanings.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Numbers in other bases have their own tool, Number bases.
  • Turning text into bytes, for example "AT\r\n" into 41 54 0D 0A, was left out on Pierre's choice. It could become a tool of its own.

How it was checked

  • A: 65, 0x41, octal 101, binary 100 0001; column 4, row 1.
  • Code 9: HT, Horizontal tab (RFC 20's name).
  • LF: 10, 0x0A, octal 012, binary 000 1010, \n, Ctrl+J.
  • Hex 7E: 126, the tilde.
  • XOFF typed by name: 19, DC3.
  • ESC: octal 033, binary 001 1011, Ctrl+[.
  • 127: DEL.
  • Out of range: 200 and é are reported as not ASCII.
  • <: shown as a character, and named less-than sign.
  • Space: shown as SP.
  • 7: 55; value = 55 − 48 = 7.
  • The chart's height: constant for all 128 characters. At 375 × 812 it ends 21 px above the tab bar.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the searchable list with RFC 20's chart, and the search with three live boxes. - It named code 9 HT, after the standard, instead of TAB. - It added names and plain meanings for the 33 control codes, C escapes, Ctrl keys, and the case and digit relations. - It escaped <, > and &, which were inserted as raw HTML. - It added examples: CR LF, XOFF/XON, a digit to its number, upper and lower case.

Digital & logic circuits › Timing & interfaces

PWM (duty cycle)

What it computes

For a pulse-width-modulated signal, the tool links six live boxes: - Frequency and Duty, the usual way to specify a PWM signal; - Ton (the pulse) and Toff (the gap), the way it is read off a scope; - High level and Low level, in volts.

From them it computes: - the average voltage, shown large; - the RMS voltage; - the period.

The waveform shows two periods, with the average as a dashed line. The slider under it sets the duty. The high and low levels are remembered.

Source

The formulas follow from the definitions. Two examples were checked against documents: - The Arduino reference for analogWrite() (reference-en, read on GitHub), which gives: - the PWM frequency: 490 Hz on most Uno, Nano and Mini pins, and 980 Hz on pins 5 and 6; - the value range: 0 (always off) to 255 (always on). - An ebm-papst DC fan catalogue page (speed setting, p. 175). It states a four-wire interface "in accordance with Intel specifications for 12 VDC fans, PWM frequency 25 kHz". Intel's own 4-wire PWM fan specification could not be opened (the copies found refused access), so it was not read.

The hobby-servo figures are the common convention, not a standard: - a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz); - 1 ms to 2 ms wide, with 1.5 ms at the centre.

What it means

PWM, pulse-width modulation, switches a signal fully on and off, fast, and sets how long it stays on. - Ton — the pulse, how long the signal stays high. - Toff — the gap, how long it stays low. - T — the period, Ton + Toff. f = 1 / T is the frequency. - The duty cycle D — the share of each period spent high, from 0 % (always off) to 100 % (always on). - The average — a load too slow to follow the switching responds to the average. That load can be a motor, a heater, the eye watching an LED, or a low-pass filter. This is how PWM sets a speed, a brightness or a DC level with a switch that wastes almost nothing: it is either fully on or fully off. - The RMS — the steady voltage that would heat a resistor the same. With a low level of 0 V, the power into a resistor is D times the full power. - A negative low level — an H-bridge switching between +V and −V. The average then goes from −V to +V as the duty goes from 0 to 100 %.

The boxes work like this: - Typing a frequency rescales the pulse and keeps the duty. - Typing a duty redistributes it and keeps the frequency. - Ton and Toff are independent, so two readings off a scope can be typed one after the other.

Why the formulas are these

D = Ton / T,   T = Ton + Toff = 1 / f
Average = Vlow + D × (Vhigh − Vlow)
RMS     = √(Vlow² × (1 − D) + Vhigh² × D)
  • The average is the time-weighted mean of the two levels: Vhigh for a share D of the time and Vlow for the rest.
  • The RMS is the square root of the time-weighted mean of the squares, by definition.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal edges. The rise and fall times are taken as zero. With real edges the average shifts a little, most at very short pulses.
  • Ideal averaging. The average is what a perfect filter, or an infinitely slow load, would see. How much ripple remains depends on the filter or the load: see the RC filter tool.
  • Frequency is a design choice the tool does not make. It must be high enough for the load to average: no visible flicker, no audible whine (20 kHz is the usual upper limit of hearing). It must also be low enough for the switching losses to stay small.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Timer register values (prescaler, top, compare) are not computed: they differ from one microcontroller family to the next.
  • Filtering the PWM into a DC level is the RC filter tool's job.

How it was checked

  • 1 kHz, 50 %, 5 V / 0 V: Ton 500 µs, average 2.5 V, RMS 3.536 V, period 1 ms.
  • 25 % at 1 kHz: 250 µs on, 750 µs off, average 1.25 V.
  • 2 kHz with the duty kept at 50 %: 250 µs on.
  • Ton 200 µs, then Toff 800 µs: 1 kHz and 20 %.
  • 150 % typed: held at 100 %, Toff 0, average 5 V.
  • +12 V / −12 V at 75 %: average 6 V, RMS 12 V.
  • Examples:
  • servo: 1.5 ms on, 18.5 ms off, 7.5 %;
  • analogWrite(128): 490 Hz, 50.2 %, 2.51 V;
  • PC fan at 40 %: 16 µs at 25 kHz;
  • 12 V motor at 75 %: 9 V.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the two mode pills with six live boxes. - It put the average voltage first and large. - It redrew the waveform: - the pulse in the part blue, not the domain colour; - two periods, with the average dashed in green; - 11 px labels instead of 9 px; - the duty slider under it. - It limited the units to real ones (Hz–MHz, ns–s), and the levels to V with a ± key. - It added plain definitions, examples, and remembered levels.

Switch debounce

(formerly Debounce / RC timing)

What it computes

It sizes the RC debouncer from Jack Ganssle's guide: Vcc through R1 to the switch, R2 from the switch to C, and C feeding a Schmitt-trigger input. - Sizing. Type the bounce time, C, Vcc and the input's worst-case thresholds (VT− at its highest, VT+ at its lowest), and R1 and R2 are sized so that both the press and the release take the bounce time to change the input. - Checking. Type R1 and R2 to check a circuit you have.

The output shows: - the delays of the circuit built from standard values, rounded up to the next value of the chosen series. The shorter delay is shown large, with the press and release delays beneath; - the two resistors in standard values; - the pressed input level caused by input leakage through R2.

Two small graphs show C's voltage after a press, falling through R2, and after a release, rising through R1 + R2. Each is drawn against the bounce window, with a dot where it crosses the threshold: green after the bounce, amber inside it. Vcc, the thresholds and the series are remembered.

Source

  • Jack Ganssle, A Guide to Debouncing, part 2 (ganssle.com) was read for:
  • the circuit;
  • the method: R2 from the press, R1 + R2 from the release, each against the worst-case threshold;
  • his worked example: 20 ms, 74AHCT14 at 5 V; with 0.1 µF R2 = 185 kΩ, and with 1 µF R2 = 18 kΩ, R1 + R2 = 101 kΩ, R1 = 82 kΩ;
  • the leakage concern;
  • his measured bounce times: most switches well under 10 ms, so he designs for 20 ms.

His equations are images on the page and could not be read as text. They were rebuilt from the RC charge law, and reproduce all three of his resistor values. - TI SN74AHCT14 datasheet (SCLS246T, October 2023) was read for the thresholds: - VT+ (rising) is 0.9–1.9 V at 4.5 V, and 1.0–2.1 V at 5.5 V; - VT− (falling) is 0.5–1.5 V at 4.5 V, and 0.6–1.7 V at 5.5 V; - Ganssle's 0.9 V and 1.7 V are the extremes; - the input current is ±1 µA. - Nexperia 74HC_HCT14 datasheet (rev. 10, 29 February 2024), table 10, was read for the 74HC14 thresholds: - at 4.5 V, VT+ is 1.7–3.15 V and VT− 0.9–2.0 V; - the input leakage is ±1.0 µA over temperature.

What it means

  • Contact bounce — a switch's contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when it is pressed or released. A fast input would see every bounce as another press.
  • The RC delay — C slows the input down. Pressing empties C through R2; releasing fills it through R1 + R2. The input changes only once C crosses its threshold, after the bouncing is over.
  • R1 — the pull-up. It also limits the current through the switch while it is held.
  • R2 — sets the press delay, and limits the current the contacts take from C.
  • Without R2 (C straight across the switch), a press registers on the very first contact, and the contacts take C's full discharge.
  • The bounce after that first contact is still filtered: an opening is too short for C to recharge past VT+ through R1.
  • A Schmitt-trigger input — it has two thresholds, VT− for a falling input and VT+ for a rising one, with a gap between them (hysteresis). So a slow, noisy edge switches it only once.
  • Ganssle warns never to feed C straight to a microcontroller input, as few have any hysteresis. An input without it does unpredictable things on a slow edge.
  • Some microcontrollers do have Schmitt-trigger inputs: check the datasheet, and use its thresholds.
  • Worst case — thresholds vary between parts and with the supply. The highest VT− and the lowest VT+ give the shortest delays, so those are the values to design with.
  • Pressed input — the input's leakage (up to 1 µA) flows through R2 while the switch is held, lifting the input up to 1 µA × R2 above ground.
  • Ganssle rejected 180 kΩ (0.18 V, against a lowest threshold of 0.5 V) and moved to 1 µF to bring R2 down to 18 kΩ.
  • The tool cautions from 0.1 V.

Why the formulas are these

Press delay   = R2 × C × ln(Vcc / VT−)
Release delay = (R1 + R2) × C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc)
Sizing:  R2 = t / (C × ln(Vcc / VT−)),   R1 + R2 = t / (C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc))
  • Press: C falls from Vcc toward 0 through R2 alone, following V = Vcc × e^(−t/R2C). It reaches VT− after R2C × ln(Vcc / VT−).
  • Release: C rises from 0 toward Vcc through R1 + R2, following V = Vcc × (1 − e^(−t/(R1+R2)C)). It reaches VT+ after (R1 + R2)C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc).
  • Bounce makes the real delays longer. Each opening during a press lets C climb back a little, so these delays are the shortest the circuit can give, which is what the design needs.
  • Typing the bounce time, C or the thresholds sizes R1 and R2. Typing R1 or R2 checks them, as typed.
  • The standard values are rounded up, so the built circuit never waits less than the bounce time. Ganssle rounded to the nearest values (18 k, 82 k): that gives 19.4 ms and 19.8 ms, a little under his 20 ms, which already doubles the bounce he measured.

Assumptions and limits

  • Full charge and discharge. Each delay starts from C fully charged or fully empty. A press released before C has emptied gives a shorter release delay.
  • Leakage only through R2 is shown. The released input also sits up to 1 µA × (R1 + R2) below Vcc.
  • Bounce time is the switch's. Measure it, or use Ganssle's 20 ms. Some switches bounce far longer.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Firmware debouncing, which Ganssle's guide also covers, is not modelled.
  • The RC charge itself, with any threshold, has its own tool: RC charge/discharge.

How it was checked

  • 20 ms, 1 µF, 74AHCT14 at 5 V (1.7 V, 0.9 V):
  • exact R2 18.539 kΩ and R1 82.242 kΩ, so R1 + R2 = 100.78 kΩ (Ganssle's 101 kΩ);
  • E24, rounded up: 20 kΩ and 91 kΩ;
  • delays: press 21.58 ms, release 22.03 ms;
  • pressed input ≤ 20 mV.
  • 0.1 µF: R2 = 185.39 kΩ (Ganssle's 185 kΩ). With 200 kΩ (E24) the pressed input sits at 200 mV, and the tool cautions.
  • 50 ms: R2 46.347 kΩ, R1 205.6 kΩ.
  • 10 k and 10 k typed with 1 µF: press 10.79 ms, release 3.969 ms, shorter than 20 ms.
  • 74HC14 at 4.5 V (2.0 V, 1.7 V), 1 µF, 20 ms: 27 kΩ and 18 kΩ (E24), shorter delay 21.35 ms.
  • R2 = 0: the press delay is 0 s, and the tool says why.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the single-resistor circuit, C straight across the switch, with Ganssle's two-resistor circuit and his worst-case method. - It made Vcc count. It was an input the result never used, because the threshold was a percentage. - It replaced the guessed 50 % threshold with VT− and VT+ in volts, from the datasheet. - It replaced the unsourced bounce-time table with Ganssle's measurements. - It added the two graphs and the leakage check. - It limited the units to real ones (Ω–MΩ, pF–µF, µs–s, volts). - It put the result first and large, added examples, and remembers the input's thresholds. - The tool was renamed Switch debounce, on Pierre's choice.

I2C pull-up resistor

What it computes

The window of pull-up resistances that work on an I²C bus, given the supply, the bus capacitance and the speed mode — and a suggested value inside it, snapped to a standard E-series.

Source

The I²C specification, NXP UM10204. Every constant here is from it: the 0.4 V output-low level, the 3 mA and 20 mA sink currents, the rise-time budgets, and the bus capacitance ceilings.

Why the formulas are these

I²C lines are open-drain. Nothing on the bus drives a line high; devices can only pull it low, and the pull-up resistor is what brings it back up. That single fact produces both bounds, pulling in opposite directions.

The lower bound is the pull-down. When a device asserts the line, its open-drain transistor has to hold it below the 0.4 V that counts as a low, and the current it must swallow is whatever the pull-up pushes through:

Rp min = (Vdd − 0.4 V) / I_OL

The spec requires devices to sink 3 mA up to Fast mode, and 20 mA in Fast mode Plus. A smaller resistor asks for more than the transistor is rated to take, and the line stops reaching a valid low.

The upper bound is the rise. Going up, the line is just an RC: the pull-up charging the bus capacitance. The spec measures rise time between 0.3 Vdd and 0.7 Vdd, and an RC charge reaches those fractions at

t(0.3 Vdd) = RC · ln(1/0.7)
t(0.7 Vdd) = RC · ln(1/0.3)

so the specified rise time is the difference:

t_r = RC · [ln(1/0.3) − ln(1/0.7)] = RC · ln(7/3) = 0.8473 · RC

Hence

Rp max = t_r / (0.8473 × Cb)

That 0.8473 is copied everywhere without explanation; it is just ln(7/3). The budget for t_r is 1000 ns at 100 kHz, 300 ns at 400 kHz and 120 ns at 1 MHz.

The suggestion is the geometric mean of the two bounds, √(Rp min × Rp max), snapped to the chosen E-series. The geometric mean is the centre of the window on a logarithmic scale, which is what "equal margin on both sides" means when the two ends can differ by a decade. For a 3.3 V standard-mode bus with 100 pF it lands on 3.3 kΩ — the value most designs actually fit.

When the window closes. Rp max falls as bus capacitance rises, while Rp min does not move. Past roughly 366 pF in Fast mode at 3.3 V the two cross and no resistor satisfies both: the bus cannot rise fast enough without asking the pull-down for more current than it is rated for. That is a real dead end, not a poor choice, and the ways out are a shorter bus, fewer devices, a slower mode, or an active bus buffer that isolates segments.

Assumptions and limits

  • Bus capacitance is an estimate. Reckon on a few pF per centimetre of track plus about 10 pF per device. It is the input people are most wrong about, and the whole upper bound scales with it. Measure it on a long bus.
  • The RC model treats the bus as one lumped capacitance and the pull-up as ideal. At Fast mode Plus, with long tracks, transmission-line behaviour starts to matter and the model flatters the real rise time.
  • Leakage from many devices and from the pull-up itself is ignored. On a bus with dozens of devices it adds a small standing current that eats into the low-level margin.
  • I_OL defaults to the spec value for the mode. A specific part may be rated differently; the field is editable for that reason.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Current-source or active pull-ups. Fast mode Plus devices sometimes use a current source rather than a resistor, which removes the RC ceiling entirely. Different circuit, different arithmetic.
  • Bus buffers and repeaters. They break a bus into segments each with their own capacitance and their own resistor; the tool sizes one segment, so run it once per segment.
  • Level shifters. A MOSFET level shifter between two voltage domains puts a pull-up on each side, and the two interact. Not modelled.

UART baud rate

What it computes

The divisor a UART needs to reach a wanted baud rate from a given peripheral clock, the rate it actually produces once that divisor is rounded to an integer, and the resulting error — with the error shown against every standard rate on the same clock.

Source

There is no single standard for baud generation: it is per-device, and the register is called BRR, UBRR, DLL/DLM or SBRG depending on whose part it is. What is common to nearly all of them is the shape — an integer divider off a peripheral clock, with the receiver oversampling each bit — and 16x oversampling, inherited from the 8250 and 16550 and still the default almost everywhere. The error budget below is derived from the sampling behaviour, not quoted.

Why the formulas are these

A UART has no oscillator of its own. It divides whatever clock it is given:

Divisor = Clock / (Oversample × Baud)

The divider is a counter, so the value written is an integer. Rounding it is the whole problem:

Actual baud = Clock / (Oversample × round(Divisor))

At 16 MHz, 115200 baud and 16x oversampling the divisor comes to 8.68. Written as 9, the line runs at 111111 baud — 3.55% slow. That single fact is why 14.7456 MHz crystals exist: 14745600 / 16 = 921600, which divides exactly into every standard rate, so the divisor is always a whole number and the error is zero. 11.0592 MHz and 18.432 MHz are the same trick at other speeds.

Why the error matters, and how much is allowed. There is no clock shared between the two ends. The receiver finds the falling edge of the start bit, starts its own counter, and samples each bit at what it believes is the middle. Take the receiver as the reference: it samples bit n at time

(n + 0.5) × T_rx

while the transmitter's bit n occupies

[ n × T_tx , (n+1) × T_tx ]

Writing r = T_tx / T_rx, the sample lands in the right bit only while

n × r  <  n + 0.5  <  (n+1) × r

Nothing resynchronises inside a frame, so the worst case is the last bit. For 8N1 that is the stop bit, n = 9:

9 r < 9.5      →  r < 1.0556
9.5 < 10 r     →  r > 0.95

So the two clocks may differ by about −5.0% to +5.56% — usually quoted as ±5%, and slightly asymmetric because the sample point is fixed at mid-bit while the bit it must land in is what stretches. That budget covers both ends together, which is why 2% each is the practical rule: it leaves room for the other end plus edge jitter and finite rise time.

Note what does not happen: the error does not accumulate across a message. The receiver re-finds the start edge on every frame, so the drift resets ten bits at a time. A 3% error is not 3% worse each byte; it is the same 3% on each of them, which is why it either works or does not.

The drawing shows exactly this. The waveform is drawn at the transmitter's real bit width, stretched or squeezed by the error, while the sample marks stay evenly spaced where the receiver puts them. Raise the error and the marks visibly walk toward the bit edges; the ones that fall outside their own bit turn red. It is the inequality above, drawn.

Assumptions and limits

  • 8N1 is assumed — one start bit, eight data, one stop, no parity. Adding parity or a second stop bit makes the frame longer and the budget tighter, since the worst case moves to a later bit.
  • The receiver is taken as exact. In reality both ends have error and the two add; the tool reports one side's, which is why the caution appears at 2% rather than 5%.
  • Integer divisors only. See below.
  • Oversampling is a divider stage, not noise immunity: 8x doubles the top speed from a given clock and halves the margin around each sample, so a noisy line suffers more.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Fractional dividers. Many modern UARTs — STM32, SAM, nRF — add fractional bits below the integer divisor, which cuts the error by roughly the resolution of that fraction and would make the numbers here pessimistic for those parts. Modelling it means picking a vendor, since the fraction is 4 bits on some parts, 6 on others, and a full 16-bit accumulator on a few.
  • Auto-baud detection, where the receiver measures a known character instead of being told the rate.
  • Anything above the physical layer: framing errors, break detection, flow control.

How it was checked

The classic cases were recomputed by hand: 16 MHz at 115200 gives divisor 8.68, used 9, 111111 baud, −3.549%; 14.7456 MHz gives exactly 8 and 0%; 16 MHz at 9600 gives 104.17, used 104, +0.160%, which is why that part runs 9600 happily and 115200 badly. 8 MHz at 115200 gives +8.507%.

The sample-point test in the drawing was checked against the inequality above at several errors: at 0% and −3.5% every sample lands inside its bit, at +0.16% likewise, and at +8.5% the last four fail — which is what n × 0.9216 < n + 0.5 predicts, the first failure being at n = 6.
